steps.body: Heaviness is measured in **grams (g)** for light things and **kilograms (kg)** for heavy ones. Anchors to keep in your pocket: a paperclip is about 1 gram; a bag of flour is about 1 kilogram. Pick the unit that keeps the number friendly.

widget.prompt: Which unit keeps each object's number friendly — grams or kilograms?

items.label: A single grape
items.feedback: A grape is a few grams — in kilograms it'd be a tiny fraction, an unfriendly number.

items.label: A watermelon
items.feedback: A watermelon is several kilograms — in grams that's thousands, clumsy to say.

items.label: A feather
items.feedback: Featherlight — well under a gram even. Grams are the small-thing unit.

items.label: A big dog
items.feedback: A big dog is tens of kilograms — the heavy-thing unit.

widget.missFeedback: Light enough to hold in your fingers → grams; heavy enough to lift with effort → kilograms.
widget.successFeedback: Grape and feather ride in grams; watermelon and dog need kilograms — the unit keeps the number comfy.

explanationVariants: An apple is heavier than a couple of paperclips but far lighter than a flour bag — about 200 grams.
Anchor it: paperclip ≈ 1 g, apple ≈ 200 g, flour bag ≈ 1,000 g. The apple sits low on that ladder.

widget.prompt: About how much does one apple weigh?

options.label: About 200 grams
options.feedback: A solid handful — a couple hundred paperclip-weights. Good gram sense.

options.label: About 200 kilograms
options.feedback: That's the weight of three grown-ups! Kilograms are the BIG unit — one apple never needs them.

options.label: About 2 grams
options.feedback: Two grams is a couple of paperclips — an apple clearly outweighs that.

options.label: About 20 kilograms
options.feedback: 20 kg is a heavy suitcase — a whole crate of apples, not one. A single apple is a couple hundred grams.

steps.body: The two units are linked by a code word: **kilo means one thousand.** So **1 kilogram = 1,000 grams** — the kilo is a thousand-badge stamped on the gram. Going kg → g, stamp on three zeros; going g → kg, peel them off.

explanationVariants: Each kilogram carries 1,000 grams, so 3 kg is 3 × 1,000 = 3,000 g.
Three thousand-badges: 3 kg → 3,000 g, just three zeros on the 3.

widget.prompt: How many grams are in 3 kilograms?

commonErrors.feedback: 300 used a hundred-badge — but kilo is the THOUSAND code. 3 kg = 3 × 1,000 = 3,000 g.
3 is the kilogram count itself — the question wants grams, and each kilo unpacks into 1,000 of them.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Kilo = 1,000. Stamp three zeros onto the 3.

steps.body: Estimate the backpack — order of magnitude.

widget.prompt: A full school backpack — about how many GRAMS? Slide to your best estimate.
widget.lowFeedback: Too light — that's pencil-case territory. A loaded backpack is heavier; slide up toward the kilograms.
widget.highFeedback: Too heavy — that's a grown adult! A backpack is a few kilograms, not tens of them.
widget.successFeedback: A few thousand grams — about 4 kg. A loaded pack sits in the low kilograms, which is thousands of grams.

predict.prompt: A full school backpack — is its mass on the 100-gram side of the line or the 10,000-gram side?
predict.reveal: A loaded backpack weighs a few kilograms — thousands of grams — landing far up toward the 10,000 mark, not near a small apple's 100.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents mass.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for mass must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines mass.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

explanationVariants: Convert to the same unit first: 2 kg = 2,000 g, which easily beats 500 g.
Don't race a kg number against a g number raw — 2 kg is 2,000 g, four times the 500 g.

widget.prompt: Which is heavier: 2 kilograms or 500 grams?

options.label: 2 kilograms
options.feedback: 2 kg = 2,000 g — four times the 500 g. Convert to one unit and it's clear.

options.label: 500 grams
options.feedback: 500 looks bigger than 2 — but they're different units! 2 kg unpacks to 2,000 g, well over 500.

options.label: They're equal
options.feedback: Equal would need 500 g to be 2 kg — but 2 kg is 2,000 g. Always match units before comparing.

options.label: Can't compare different units
options.feedback: You can — just convert first. 2 kg → 2,000 g, then compare to 500 g: the kilograms win.

hints: The units don't match yet — fix that first.
Then add the crate's kilograms to that.
explanationVariants: Convert first: 2,000 g = 2 kg. Then 5 kg + 2 kg = 7 kg total.
Same amount, two costumes: the bananas are 2 kg, so the crate holds 5 + 2 = 7 kg.

widget.prompt: A crate holds 5 kg of apples. A grocer adds 2,000 g of bananas. What is the total mass, in KILOGRAMS?

commonErrors.feedback: 2005 glued a kg number to a g number — unit glue! Convert the 2,000 g to 2 kg first, then add: 5 + 2.
7,000 is the right amount in GRAMS (5,000 + 2,000). But the question asks kilograms: 7 kg.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Convert 2,000 g to kg, then add to the 5 kg.

steps.body: You've got a feel for mass.
takeaways: Grams for light things, kilograms for heavy — keep the number friendly.
Match units before you compare or add.
steps.teaser: next: from how HEAVY to how MUCH — measuring liquid in liters.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **Kilo is a thousand-badge** — it works the same on every unit. A kiloGRAM is 1,000 grams, a kiloMETER is 1,000 meters. To go from the big unit to the small one, stamp on three zeros.

explanationVariants: One kilogram carries its thousand grams: 1 kg = 1,000 g.
The kilo-badge is worth three zeros — stamp them onto the 1.

options.label: 100 grams
options.feedback: 100 is the CENTI code (a hundredth). Kilo is the thousand: 1,000 g.

options.label: 10 grams
options.feedback: Ten grams is a couple of coins. A whole kilogram packs a thousand grams.
